Quadratic weights and uniqueness at infinity

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI) and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI). Self-checked by the writing AI. Original exposition: CC0.

Working question: Which decay hypothesis can force a positive-energy solution to vanish? The quadratic radius is determined by the operator, so an indefinite form supplies a cone rather than a Euclidean ball. Near its null boundary the potential may obey a different bound. The finite-weight theorem exposes the exact threshold and the boundary-layer limit, making clear why a solution with only an insufficient decay weight cannot be discarded.

Positive energy supplies a useful sign even when the angular part of a differential operator has no sign. A power of the radius exposes this through a commutator. For an indefinite quadratic operator, the appropriate radius exists only inside a cone. We will prove the estimate there, remove a cutoff next to the cone boundary, and then translate the cone to reach every point.

The distinction between an elliptic radius and an indefinite one matters for the potential. The indefinite result permits slower decay near the null cone. For further reading, see Kato's Growth properties of solutions of the reduced wave equation with a variable coefficient, Russian translation and Koch–Tataru [KT], Section 3, on logarithmic radial coordinates and conjugated operators.

The coordinate and measure inputs are proved in Coordinate inverses and integration, CI1–CI7 and finite localization. The smoothing, weak product rule and graph approximations use Approximation and convolution, Theorems 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1. Fourier inversion and Plancherel are proved in the Fourier foundation; the compact-distribution transform is also constructed in Mild weights and frequency localization. Every use of spectral calculus in Example 3.2 has the earlier self-adjoint domain proof.

An orthogonal coordinate change diagonalizes GGG; it preserves Euclidean measure and the displayed quadratic operator. For comparison, this is the finite-dimensional case of Hilbert spaces and compact operators, Theorem 6.2. Its eigenvector construction can be made real: for a real matrix and real eigenvalue, a nonzero real or imaginary part of a complex eigenvector is a real eigenvector. Its real orthogonal complement is invariant; repeat there. Invertibility excludes zero eigenvalues. Here is also a direct real finite-dimensional proof. The quadratic function q(e)=eTGeq(e)=e^TGeq(e)=eTGe attains its maximum on the real unit sphere, by finite-dimensional compactness. At a maximizing unit vector eee, differentiate q((e+th)/∣e+th∣)q((e+th)/|e+th|)q((e+th)/∣e+th∣) at t=0t=0t=0 for any h⊥eh\perp eh⊥e. The derivative is 2hTGe2h^TGe2hTGe, hence zero. Symmetry makes e⊥e^\perpe⊥ invariant; repeating on this real subspace gives an orthonormal eigenbasis by induction on its dimension, with the one-dimensional case immediate. Zero cannot be an eigenvalue of an invertible matrix. An orthogonal matrix has determinant of absolute value one by QTQ=IQ^TQ=IQTQ=I, so the change of variables preserves the stated measure. This supplies the diagonalization used in (5) without invoking an infinite-dimensional theorem.

For a self-adjoint Schrödinger operator −Δ+W-\Delta+W−Δ+W, set V=−WV=-WV=−W. If a positive-energy eigenfunction has (16) and WWW has (17), it vanishes. In particular, whenever Limiting absorption and point spectrum gives rapid weighted decay for every eigenfunction at a positive regular energy of a real short-range potential with this bound, that energy has no eigenfunction. The rapid decay hypothesis is part of the implication; an arbitrary L2L^2L2 solution has not been substituted for it.

Example 3.2 (an inverse-radius potential with a bound state). The decay of the solution in Corollary 3.1 matters. We construct a real smooth potential WWW on R3\mathbb R^3R3 with ∣W(x)∣≤C/(1+∣x∣)|W(x)|\leq C/(1+|x|)∣W(x)∣≤C/(1+∣x∣) for which −Δ+W-\Delta+W−Δ+W has eigenvalue one inside its positive essential spectrum. This is a von Neumann–Wigner type construction. The classical example and its relativistic extensions are discussed by József Lőrinczi and Itaru Sasaki in Embedded eigenvalues and Neumann–Wigner potentials for relativistic Schrödinger operators, Section 1. We verify the normalization and all the properties used here directly.

differentiate w=sin⁡r/Fw=\sin r/Fw=sinr/F twice. Where sin⁡r≠0\sin r\ne0sinr=0, the result is

5. Translating cones to prove global uniqueness

Theorem 5.1 (indefinite quadratic uniqueness). Let GGG be real symmetric, invertible and indefinite, and let A,BA,BA,B be (1). Suppose λ∈R∖{0}\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}λ∈R∖{0}, uuu has (16), and

(B(∂)+λ+V)u=0,∣V(x)∣≤C(∣A(x)∣+1+∣x∣)−1/2a.e.(27) (B(\partial)+\lambda+V)u=0, \qquad |V(x)|\leq C\bigl(|A(x)|+1+|x|\bigr)^{-1/2} \quad\text{a.e.} \tag{27} (B(∂)+λ+V)u=0,∣V(x)∣≤C(∣A(x)∣+1+∣x∣)−1/2a.e.(27)

Then u=0u=0u=0 almost everywhere on Rn\mathbb R^nRn. The potential may be complex.

Proof. First suppose λ>0\lambda>0λ>0. For every fixed center yyy, the translated form satisfies

A(x−y)=A(x)−2xTG−1y+A(y),∣A(x−y)∣≤Cy(∣A(x)∣+1+∣x∣).(28) A(x-y)=A(x)-2x^TG^{-1}y+A(y), \qquad |A(x-y)|\leq C_y\bigl(|A(x)|+1+|x|\bigr). \tag{28} A(x−y)=A(x)−2xTG−1y+A(y),∣A(x−y)∣≤Cy​(∣A(x)∣+1+∣x∣).(28)

Thus A(x−y)∣V(x)∣2A(x-y)|V(x)|^2A(x−y)∣V(x)∣2 is bounded on Oy={x:A(x−y)>0}O_y=\{x:A(x-y)>0\}Oy​={x:A(x−y)>0}. For each center, choose a possibly center-dependent exponent s≥max⁡(1,Ky/(4λ))s\geq\max(1,K_y/(4\lambda))s≥max(1,Ky​/(4λ)), where Ky=ess supOyA(x−y)∣V(x)∣2K_y=\mathop{\mathrm{ess\,sup}}_{O_y}A(x-y)|V(x)|^2Ky​=esssupOy​​A(x−y)∣V(x)∣2. Translation preserves (16), because for fixed y,sy,sy,s the ratios of (1+∣x∣)s(1+|x|)^s(1+∣x∣)s and (1+∣x−y∣)s(1+|x-y|)^s(1+∣x−y∣)s are bounded in both directions. It preserves the constant differential operator. Lemma 4.1 in coordinates x−yx-yx−y therefore proves u=0u=0u=0 almost everywhere on OyO_yOy​.

A countable collection of these cones covers the space. Since GGG is indefinite, choose zzz with A(z)>0A(z)>0A(z)>0. For any xxx, the center y0=x−zy_0=x-zy0​=x−z has A(x−y0)>0A(x-y_0)>0A(x−y0​)>0. By continuity, the same holds for some rational center y∈Qny\in\mathbb Q^ny∈Qn sufficiently close to y0y_0y0​. Hence ⋃y∈QnOy=Rn\bigcup_{y\in\mathbb Q^n}O_y=\mathbb R^n⋃y∈Qn​Oy​=Rn. The exceptional null sets from the separate cone arguments still have null countable union, which proves the conclusion.

For λ<0\lambda<0λ<0, multiply the equation by −1-1−1. The new data are

G′=−G,B′=−B,A′=−A,λ′=−λ>0,V′=−V.(29) G'=-G,\quad B'=-B,\quad A'=-A,\quad \lambda'=-\lambda>0,\quad V'=-V. \tag{29} G′=−G,B′=−B,A′=−A,λ′=−λ>0,V′=−V.(29)

The matrix G′G'G′ remains indefinite and invertible. Its dual form is exactly −A-A−A, and ∣A′∣=∣A∣|A'|=|A|∣A′∣=∣A∣ preserves (27). Apply the positive-energy result to these data. □\square□

The constants KyK_yKy​ obtained from (28) need not be uniformly bounded in yyy. The fixed-cone improvement has therefore not replaced Theorem 5.1’s rapid hypothesis by one universal finite exponent. Its sign reversal and countable rational-center cover retain their stated scope. For a negative definite matrix at negative energy, sign reversal separately gives the matching definite result with G′=−GG'=-GG′=−G, A′=−AA'=-AA′=−A, and V′=−VV'=-VV′=−V.

V(x)=(∣x12−x22∣+1+∣x∣)−1/2(30) V(x)=\bigl(|x_1^2-x_2^2|+1+|x|\bigr)^{-1/2} \tag{30} V(x)=(∣x12​−x22​∣+1+∣x∣)−1/2(30)

satisfies (27). On the null ray x=(t,t)x=(t,t)x=(t,t), t→+∞t\to+\inftyt→+∞, it is comparable to t−1/2t^{-1/2}t−1/2. On a fixed ray x=tωx=t\omegax=tω with A(ω)≠0A(\omega)\ne0A(ω)=0, it is comparable to t−1t^{-1}t−1. The top panel draws the exact dual form in Example 1.2: shading denotes A>0A>0A>0, and the hyperbolas have radii r=1,2r=1,2r=1,2. The dashed null lines form the boundary where this radius vanishes. The estimate and the uniqueness theorem use different kinds of support. The estimate begins with support compactly inside a cone. The uniqueness theorem begins with a global weak H1H^1H1 solution and removes both the unbounded outer region and the layer next to the cone boundary. The finite-weight proof fixes sss, removes the outer cutoff, and then lets the boundary layer shrink, retaining the radial derivative at the threshold. The alternative rapid-decay proof instead uses the uniform constant in (25) before taking its increasing-weight limit.

Use the conclusion

Check the equality case of the weight threshold and the translated-cone argument. Compare the bound-state counterexample with the sufficient finite-weight hypothesis; keep the complex-potential scope and the separate rapid-decay alternative.

6. Exercises and checked solutions

Exercise 6.1 (foundation). In the hyperbolic model (8), compute dμd\mudμ on both branches, the Jacobian of x=(σrcosh⁡s,rsinh⁡s)x=(\sigma r\cosh s,r\sinh s)x=(σrcoshs,rsinhs), and the operator (9). Explain why the angular quadratic form has the opposite sign from the Euclidean sphere's.

Exercise 6.2 (intermediate). Let uuu have compact support K⋐OK\Subset OK⋐O, u∈L2u\in L^2u∈L2, and (B(∂)+λ)u∈L2(B(\partial)+\lambda)u\in L^2(B(∂)+λ)u∈L2. Prove that convolution approximates both graph entries with support in one compact subset of OOO. Explain why this proves (10) for each fixed τ\tauτ, and why it makes no assertion of uniform approximation as τ→∞\tau\to\inftyτ→∞.

Exercise 6.3 (intermediate). For the potential (30), prove that no constant gives ∣V(x)∣≤C/∣x∣|V(x)|\leq C/|x|∣V(x)∣≤C/∣x∣ for all large xxx. Nevertheless, give an explicit upper bound for sup⁡OyA(x−y)∣V(x)∣2\sup_{O_y}A(x-y)|V(x)|^2supOy​​A(x−y)∣V(x)∣2 in terms of y,Gy,Gy,G.

Exercise 6.4 (advanced). Derive (21) directly in Cartesian coordinates, without using polar coordinates. Prove the exponent τ/2−1\tau/2-1τ/2−1 in (25). Then explain why a bound obtained before removing the outer cutoff at fixed τ\tauτ would not, by itself, justify taking τ→∞\tau\to\inftyτ→∞ in (26).

Exercise 6.5 (advanced). Put u(x)=sech⁡xu(x)=\operatorname{sech}xu(x)=sechx on the line. Find λ<0\lambda<0λ<0 and a real smooth VVV with ∣V(x)∣≤C/∣x∣|V(x)|\leq C/|x|∣V(x)∣≤C/∣x∣ such that (∂x2+λ+V)u=0(\partial_x^2+\lambda+V)u=0(∂x2​+λ+V)u=0. Verify (16). Identify the precise reason that sign reversal does not extend Corollary 3.1 to this example, although sign reversal is valid in Theorem 5.1.

Solution 6.1. On either branch,

∣ω′(s)∣=sinh⁡2s+cosh⁡2s=∣G−1ω(s)∣,dS=∣ω′∣ ds. |\omega'(s)|=\sqrt{\sinh^2s+\cosh^2s} =|G^{-1}\omega(s)|, \qquad dS=|\omega'|\,ds. ∣ω′(s)∣=sinh2s+cosh2s​=∣G−1ω(s)∣,dS=∣ω′∣ds.

Formula (3) gives dμ=dsd\mu=dsdμ=ds. The absolute Jacobian is r∣σ(cosh⁡2s−sinh⁡2s)∣=rr|\sigma(\cosh^2s-\sinh^2s)|=rr∣σ(cosh2s−sinh2s)∣=r, so dx=r dr dsdx=r\,dr\,dsdx=rdrds on each branch. The inverse first derivatives are

∂1=σcosh⁡s ∂r−σr−1sinh⁡s ∂s,∂2=−sinh⁡s ∂r+r−1cosh⁡s ∂s. \partial_1=\sigma\cosh s\,\partial_r -\sigma r^{-1}\sinh s\,\partial_s, \qquad \partial_2=-\sinh s\,\partial_r+r^{-1}\cosh s\,\partial_s. ∂1​=σcoshs∂r​−σr−1sinhs∂s​,∂2​=−sinhs∂r​+r−1coshs∂s​.

Squaring these fields includes derivatives of their coefficients. Their mixed second derivatives cancel in ∂12−∂22\partial_1^2-\partial_2^2∂12​−∂22​; their radial second coefficient is one, angular second coefficient −r−2-r^{-2}−r−2, and remaining first coefficients are r−1r^{-1}r−1 radially and zero angularly. This gives (9). Integration by parts yields (−∂s2f,f)=∥f′∥2( -\partial_s^2f,f)=\|f'\|^2(−∂s2​f,f)=∥f′∥2, whereas the sphere Laplacian satisfies (ΔSf,f)=−∥∇Sf∥2(\Delta_S f,f)=-\|\nabla_S f\|^2(ΔS​f,f)=−∥∇S​f∥2.

Solution 6.2. The compact set KKK has positive distance from the complement of OOO. Choose δ>0\delta>0δ>0 smaller than this distance and choose a smooth mollifier supported in the ball of radius one. Convolution at radii less than δ/2\delta/2δ/2 has support in K+B‾δ/2⋐OK+\overline B_{\delta/2}\Subset OK+Bδ/2​⋐O. Constant coefficients give

(B(∂)+λ)(u∗ρη)=((B(∂)+λ)u)∗ρη. (B(\partial)+\lambda)(u*\rho_\eta) =((B(\partial)+\lambda)u)*\rho_\eta. (B(∂)+λ)(u∗ρη​)=((B(∂)+λ)u)∗ρη​.

Both entries converge in L2L^2L2 by the approximate identity property. For fixed τ\tauτ, the two positive weights in (10) are bounded on the common compact set, so the weighted norms converge as well. Apply the smooth estimate and take η→0\eta\to0η→0. Bounds for the weights on that compact set can grow exponentially with τ\tauτ; this reasoning fixes τ\tauτ before smoothing and supplies no uniform approximation for a varying τ\tauτ.

Solution 6.3. On x=(t,t)x=(t,t)x=(t,t), ∣x∣V(x)=2t(1+2t)−1/2→∞|x|V(x)=\sqrt2t(1+\sqrt2t)^{-1/2}\to\infty∣x∣V(x)=2​t(1+2​t)−1/2→∞. The asserted uniform inverse-radius bound therefore fails. On any translated positive cone, (28) and the explicit formula for VVV give

A(x−y)∣A(x)∣+1+∣x∣≤1+2∣G−1y∣+∣A(y)∣. \frac{A(x-y)}{|A(x)|+1+|x|} \leq 1+2|G^{-1}y|+|A(y)|. ∣A(x)∣+1+∣x∣A(x−y)​≤1+2∣G−1y∣+∣A(y)∣.

Indeed the three numerator terms are bounded by ∣A(x)∣|A(x)|∣A(x)∣, 2∣G−1y∣∣x∣2|G^{-1}y||x|2∣G−1y∣∣x∣, and ∣A(y)∣|A(y)|∣A(y)∣, respectively, and each is bounded by its displayed coefficient times the common denominator. The supremum in the question is at most this finite quantity. No bound uniform in all centers is needed.

Solution 6.4. For a smooth multiplier mmm,

[B(∂),m]u=(B(∂)m)u+2(G∇m)⋅∇u. [B(\partial),m]u=(B(\partial)m)u +2(G\nabla m)\cdot\nabla u. [B(∂),m]u=(B(∂)m)u+2(G∇m)⋅∇u.

Take m=ψ(A/ε)m=\psi(A/\varepsilon)m=ψ(A/ε). Since G∇A=2xG\nabla A=2xG∇A=2x, B(∂)A=2nB(\partial)A=2nB(∂)A=2n, and (∇A)TG∇A=4A(\nabla A)^TG\nabla A=4A(∇A)TG∇A=4A, the chain rule gives exactly (21). On its support A≤2εA\leq2\varepsilonA≤2ε, all coefficients multiplying uuu are bounded by C/εC/\varepsilonC/ε, and the last term is bounded by C∣x∣∣∇u∣/εC|x||\nabla u|/\varepsilonC∣x∣∣∇u∣/ε. After squaring, multiplying by A1+τ/2A^{1+\tau/2}A1+τ/2, and integrating, the factor is ε−2(2ε)1+τ/2=4(2ε)τ/2−1\varepsilon^{-2}(2\varepsilon)^{1+\tau/2}=4(2\varepsilon)^{\tau/2-1}ε−2(2ε)1+τ/2=4(2ε)τ/2−1. The remaining weighted first-derivative norm of uuu is finite by (16) and independent of the two parameters. This proves (25), after the potential term is absorbed. The outer error (24) contains RτR^\tauRτ and constants depending on τ\tauτ. Rapid decay makes it tend to zero for each fixed τ\tauτ; it does not furnish a limit uniform over all positive τ\tauτ at a fixed RRR. Therefore the justified order is R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞ first and τ→∞\tau\to\inftyτ→∞ afterward.

Solution 6.5. Direct differentiation gives

u′=−utanh⁡x,u′′=(1−2sech⁡2x)u. u'=-u\tanh x,\qquad u''=(1-2\operatorname{sech}^2x)u. u′=−utanhx,u′′=(1−2sech2x)u.

Thus λ=−1\lambda=-1λ=−1, V=2sech⁡2xV=2\operatorname{sech}^2xV=2sech2x solve the equation. Both uuu and u′u'u′ decay exponentially at either end, so every polynomial multiple is square integrable. The function 2∣x∣sech⁡2x2|x|\operatorname{sech}^2x2∣x∣sech2x is bounded: it is continuous, vanishes at zero, and tends to zero at infinity. This verifies (17). Here G=1G=1G=1 is positive definite. Sign reversal produces G′=−1G'=-1G′=−1 and A′(x)=−x2A'(x)=-x^2A′(x)=−x2, whose positive cone is empty. The cone estimate with positive energy has nowhere to apply. In the indefinite theorem, both GGG and −G-G−G have nonempty positive cones, so this obstruction does not arise. The positive sign in the elliptic energy assumption is essential.
